thag21.1:32.2: The idea of the seven seers, long proverbial in Vedic culture, was adapted for Gotama in [dn14](), where he is the seventh recorded Buddha in the lineage starting with Vipassī. Various texts and commentaries also allow the sense, “best of seers”.
thag21.1:32.4: In a cold northern climate this sounds unappealing, but in the heat the generous rain is a cool blessing.
thag21.1:34.1: The “wrong path” (_ummagga_) is one that takes you to the wrong destination ([mn107:14.26]()).
thag21.1:34.2: [sn8.8:8.2]() has the second person _carasi_, and it seems reasonable to assume that Vaṅgīsa is continuing to address the Buddha directly. | From the same place accept the reading _khila_ rather than _khīla_.
thag21.1:34.3: Here Vaṅgīsa turns to address the monks directly.
thag21.1:34.4: For _asitaṁ bhāgaso pavibhajaṁ_, compare the similar phrase _vibhatto bhāgaso mito_, which refers to the neatly ordered sections of hell ([mn130:16.4]()) or the suburbs ([snp2.7:23.2]()). Vaṅgīsa is referring to the Buddha’s skill in breaking down complex or obscure matters and presenting them systematically.
thag21.1:35.3: These lines follow Bodhi’s reading at [sn8.8:9.3]().
thag21.1:36.2: _Ṭhiti_ is _viññāṇaṭṭhiti_ (“planes of consciousness”), i.e. seven realms in which consciousness can be reborn ([an7.44](), [dn15:33.1](), [dn33:1.8.11]()). This is a subtle allusion to the Buddha’s practice under his former teacher Āḷāra Kālāma, where he learned up to the highest “plane of consciousness”, namely the dimension of nothingness. In [snp5.15:3.1]() he speaks of how he understood that attainment and went beyond it. | Not to be confused with the four “grounds for consciousness”, i.e. the first four aggregates, as insight does *not* consist in going beyond these to consciousness ([dn33:1.11.122](), [sn22.54:1.11]()).
thag21.1:36.4: Vaṅgīsa continues to invoke the Buddha’s life story by alluding to the first teaching, Rolling Forth the Wheel of Dhamma ([sn56.11]()). After leaving behind those who taught rebirth in the “planes of consciousness”, the Buddha realized Awakening and proceeded to Varanasi to teach the group of five. This anticipates the next verses, which feature one of the five.
thag21.1:38.1: Spoken at [sn8.9:3.1](), while the first two lines are included in Koṇḍañña’s verses at [thag21.1:38.1]().
thag21.1:38.2: Koṇḍañña was the first person to realize the Dhamma after the Buddha ([sn56.11:14.3]()). He features rarely in the early texts, but the Buddha once saw him meditating ([ud7.6]()), and praised him as the senior mendicant ([an1.188:1.1]()).
thag21.1:43.1: Emend _anekākārasampannaṁ_ to _anekākārasampannā_ per Bodhi’s *Connected Discourses*, note 527.
thag21.1:45.1: This verse is plural, presumably referring to a troupe of wandering bards. | For “drunk on poetry” see [sn4.13:2.1]() and note.
thag21.1:63.3: _Kāmakāro_: “wish-granter”. Ordinary people cannot simply get what they want.
thag21.1:63.4: _Saṅkheyyakāro_: “comprehensibility-granter”. _Saṅkheyya_ is “calculable, comprehensible”, not “after comprehension”. The Buddha has a gift for explaining things in a way that makes them comprehensible.
